questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to travel outside Europe, preferably North America, and Canada seemed the obvious choice. From other students I had heard a lot of great things about Montreal as a city and about McGill University. It was important to me that I lived in a city with lots to do, as opposed to living on a campus in the middle of nowhere.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was an experience I will of course never forget, and I am very happy I did it. Some of my courses on McGill were however not that good, which is why I'm rating it 8/10.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. As soon as you have created your McGill e-mail, you will get a lot of information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The coordinator for SCIENCE exchange at McGill, Mary, had an introductory meeting with all exchange students at the science faculty of McGill, and she really wanted to have a private meeting with each of us, talking about the courses we got and if we needed any assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I found it pretty easy, Montreal is a very livable city compared to other Canadian cities like Toronto and Vancouver. Many students are subletting an extra room or an entire apartment. 

I found housing through a big Facebook site called McGill Off-Campus housing. There are of course a few scammers on this site, but you should just use common sense and get a virtual tour of the place.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
The metro in Montreal is very very good, and McGill has its own stops (station McGill and station Peel). I think a new line is opening in 2023 as well. We lived nicely close to campus (about 10 minutes on bike), so we didn't really take the metro, but we knew others who did. 

Students can purchase 1-month unlimited travel in metro and buses for 56 dollars (around 290 kr)

So unless your off campus place is close to the campus, just make sure its close to a metro station.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Our place was not that amazing (it didn't have a lot of windows), but it was very cheap and our landlord was nice.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Course registration begins in June, and courses fill up fast, so beforehand you should make a list of the ones you want the most. 

Registration itself happens on Minerva (McGill Absalon). You go to the registration page and write the course registration code for up to five courses in a field, and then you press enter.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Exchange advisor you could write to, and many emails explaining the process.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: As mentioned, I did not get two courses that I wanted, so I had to take some of my plan B courses (one of which was very bad), so it was a bit of a letdown.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Some of the courses I wanted to take I did not get, so the day before the course registration opens for exchange students, you should check which courses are full and act accordingly. I did however get into a course that was full by writing to the professor. Sometimes they let you in.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Third year courses at McGill (300-level) are very basic and therefore a bit boring (I had to write an assignment about what a Western blot is, which is a method we learn in our first year at KU). 

The fourth year courses (400 level) were much better, and much more like the ones at KU. We had lectures and then read articles related to that lecture and so on. 400 level courses are however a bit harder, with term papers and so on, so I would recommend doing two or three 400-level courses, and then take at least one easy introductory French course to have a 'relaxing' course.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: At McGill there are no SAU or TØ classes, there are only lectures. In 400-levels, fewer people are registered (25-35), so the lectures function a bit as SAU and TØ. I did not like that we only had lectures, as I very much like the classroom setting.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
PHAR 300 Drug Action
Supposedly an introduction to pharmacology and how drugs (both 'fun' drugs and actual prescription drugs) work and effect the body. The course is however very bad, with a horrible professor. She spends most of the lecture talking about statistics for the drug use or goes on long rants about how much she hates cigarettes, alcohol, cannabis, cosmetics, essential oils, herbal medicine and Chinese traditional medicine. Then on the exam there are very specific questions about the mechanism of action of very specific drugs, some which are not mentioned in the lecture. She also does not share her slides, as she is paranoid about copyright.

MIMM 324 Fundamental Virology
Very fundamental course about viruses, you need to learn about a lot of irrelevant small viruses you've never heard of before and much of their replication cycle. There are also a few viruses you learn about much more in depth (HPV, hepatitis C and HIV) which is much more interesting. 

PHGY 488 Stem Cell Biology
A course about stem cells. Very good course and it was the most KU-like course I had at McGill. You do a presentation on an article and write a paper about another article. 

PHGY 518 Artificial Cells
An interesting course taught by the founder of the field, who is almost 90 years old. For the same reason, the course has few lectures and is mostly you doing a presentation and 10-page paper on a topic you decide yourself within the field of artificial cells. It is however very interesting.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend PHGY 488 Stem Cell Biology, even if you aren't interested in stem cells (which I wasn't), as you learn a lot of relevant information and get training in presenting and writing about scientific articles. 

I would also recommend PHGY 518, though I doubt Thomas Chang will continue to be in the course much longer (he is very old), just be prepared that you don't learn that much, and have to do a lot of work. There is no exam though, which is nice. 

I would NOT recommend PHAR 300, avoid at all cost. It is draining and frustrating.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Phone service is VERY VERY expensive in Canada. 3 GB of data each month costs around 120 kr. I had an e-sim plan, which worked fine, but I has to use Whatsapp and messenger for telephoning.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The Quebec Health insurance, RAMQ, is free for Danish students. Just register at RAMQ website and you get a health insurance card. You can't do it before you arrive in Canada though, and then the card itself comes after a few weeks. For the same reason, you don't have to buy the official McGill health insurance, which is quite expensive, you can just request and exemption.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There is a gym with a rather cheap membership and a free 25 meter pool. 

Socially I would recommend joining the McGill outdoor club and the knitting club.

There are a few introductory arrangements at McGill, namely 'Frosh', which is for their first-year students. Keep in mind that in America you start university at 17. Therefore, the official McGill frosh I registered for (and paid 1000 kr for) was not that great, as the other people were very young. 

Other people went on the Outdoor frosh, with activities such as camping and hiking. Here there were more exchange students and older students, which I regret I did not register for as well.

A student organization called MustBus arranges cheap bus trips to other parts of Canada and the US. My roommates and I went to Toronto for a few days, a very fun experience.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Rent a car and drive to the national parks surrounding Montreal, the nature is amazing, especially in the autumn! Especially Mont Tremblant and Mont Megantic. Otherwise, Parc Mont-Saint Bruno is reachable by metro and then a bus for 30 minutes. I can also recommend taking a day trip to Vermont or upstate New York.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Natural Parks or trips to Toronto and Quebec City. 

I went to New York City in my Christmas break and my family came over. That was great as well. The Greyhound bus between Montreal and NYC is very nice and relatively cheap, if you can tolerate the 9 hour bus drive.

In the every day life, you should check out St. Viateur Bagels, they are so delicious (only cash payment!)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, Montreal is a very european city.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
I was not that succesful in this, but you should come to the McGill clubs like outdoor club and knitting club. If you live in the McGill dorms you will have much more contact with other exchange students.

Many students aren't from Quebec and don't speak French.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There weren't really any, except that local students at McGill really study a lot, so they don't have a lot of free time.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: That it was so French, it was very strange but very nice (plus their croissants were amazing).

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Find housing before you arrive.

Bring warm clothes.

Go to Saint-Viateur bagels with lots of cash.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
BIXI bikes are cheap city bikes, and as Montreal is a very bike friendly city, it is a great way to get around.

The cold and snow comes in end-November, but I was lucky as it was a very mild year.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing Quebec and North American Culture.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Having four courses at the same time.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
